carinthiasuchus:abstract:1.title: CARINTHIASUCHUS KANDUTSCHI, A NEW ARCHOSAUR (REPTILIA: DIAPSIDA) FROM THE TRIASSIC OF AUSTRIA (abstract)

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was discovered by Georg Kandutsch near Jadersdorf in the Gailtal Alps of Carinthia, Austria.
facts.quote: The specimen was discovered by Georg Kandutsch near the village of Jadersdorf in the Gailtal Alps of Carinthia in southern Austria.

facts.statement: The species is known from a single holotype specimen containing parts of the skull, caudal vertebrae, and an articulated distal tail.
facts.quote: Carinthiasuchus kandutschi is known from a single specimen, holotype Nockalm 7030u, a slab of limestone containing parts of the skull, a collection of caudal vertebrae, and a more distal part of the tail still preserved in articulation.

facts.statement: The specific name kandutschi honors the animal's discoverer, Georg Kandutsch.
facts.quote: The specific name meanwhile was chosen in honor of the animal's discoverer, Georg Kandutsch.

facts.statement: Carinthiasuchus lived during the Ladinian to Carnian stages of the Triassic period.
This animal lived in the Partnach Formation of Carinthia, Austria, from the Ladinian to Early Carnian ages.
facts.quote: Carinthiasuchus is an extinct genus of poposauroid pseudosuchian from the Ladinian to Early Carnian Partnach Formation of Carinthia, Austria.

facts.statement: The preserved skull measures 53 mm, leading to an estimated total body length of up to 65 mm for the juvenile specimen.
facts.quote: The preserved portion measures approximately 53 mm, which Dalla Vecchia and Cau use as the basis for an estimated total length of perhaps up to 65 mm when considering the fact that the premaxilla was rather short.

facts.statement: The lack of fusion in certain vertebrae and skull bones indicates that the holotype specimen was not fully mature.
facts.quote: While some of the vertebrae in the distal tail region are already fused, other more proximal vertebrae, the skull bones, and the mandibular symphysis are not, indicating that the individual was not yet fully mature.

facts.statement: The animal possessed a distinct series of bony plates, or osteoderms, running down its tail.
facts.quote: Carinthiasuchus still preserves a distinct series of bony plates running down its tail.

facts.statement: The tail osteoderms were drop-shaped, longer than wide, and featured a midline ridge with denticles on their irregular outer margins.
facts.quote: The individual osteoderms are longer than wide, drop-shaped, bear a ridge running down their midline but are otherwise relatively smooth and symmetrical with irregular outer margins featuring pronounced denticles.

facts.statement: The osteoderms were arranged in a double row along the spine, with each vertebra corresponding to two or three pairs of plates.
facts.quote: These osteoderms, which in life would have been positioned along the spine, are arranged in pairs to form a double row, with each vertebra roughly corresponding to two or three osteoderm pairs along the tail.

facts.statement: Carinthiasuchus is classified as a member of the clade Poposauroidea.
Phylogenetic analyses place Carinthiasuchus as a member of the early-diverging clade Poposauroidea within Pseudosuchia.
facts.quote: The phylogenetic analyses conducted by Dalla Vecchia and Cau recover Carinthiasuchus as a member of the clade Poposauroidea, an early branch of Pseudosuchia well known for its great morphological diversity.

facts.statement: Studies indicate that placing Carinthiasuchus in Poposauroidea is more optimal than linking it to other European crocodylomorphs or rauisuchians.
facts.quote: Attempts to force a relationship with other European crocodylomorphs like Batrachotomus, Polonosuchus and Ticinosuchus have furthermore shown that its placement in Poposauroidea is the most optimal outcome, with rauisuchian affinities being less likely.

facts.statement: The type locality for the species is the Partnach Formation.
The fossils were found in Austria.
The taxon Carinthiasuchus is currently considered valid.
The description represents a new genus and new species.
